power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

The growing uses and applications of generative artificial intelligence (AI) have been changing the actions and academic behaviors of learners and educators in higher education (Freeman, 2025; Watson & Ennion, 2026).
text.formatted: The growing uses and applications of generative artificial intelligence (AI) have been changing the actions and academic behaviors of learners and educators in higher education <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Freeman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Watson & Ennion, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: AI has introduced new time-efficient ways for doing academic tasks.
In the example of completing an essay assignment, AI can help with structuring arguments, synthesizing sources, conducting literature research, and even the writing itself (Freeman, 2025).
text.formatted: In the example of completing an essay assignment, AI can help with structuring arguments, synthesizing sources, conducting literature research, and even the writing itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Freeman, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Asking AI to search and synthesize the most cited and relevant studies related to a research question can be more appealing time-wise, when compared with manually identifying individual related papers and reading through and searching them for the potentially numerous answers to the initial research question.
Many similar comparisons can be made for other educational tasks such as writing a specific part of a paper or meticulously preparing a table based on APA.

In terms of how the use of AI has influenced learners so far, previous findings are not encouraging. Fan et al. (2025) highlighted that reliance on generative AI can be conducive to dependence on it, leading to what the authors termed as "metacognitive laziness" (p. 490).
text.formatted: In terms of how the use of AI has influenced learners so far, previous findings are not encouraging. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fan et al. (2025)</ref> highlighted that reliance on generative AI can be conducive to dependence on it, leading to what the authors termed as "metacognitive laziness" (p. 490).

text.text: It involves not expending the effort in metacognitive processes (e.g., evaluation, orientation) during task revision, that is a prerequisite for deep and durable learning.

Similarly, other studies have shown that over-reliance on AI and excessive use of it are associated with a decrease in critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning (Gerlich, 2025; Tian & Zhang, 2025; Zhai et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, other studies have shown that over-reliance on AI and excessive use of it are associated with a decrease in critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gerlich, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Tian & Zhang, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Zhai et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: There seems to be an "efficiency-understanding" trade-off among learners. Abbas et al. (2024) showed that, when students realized that AI assistance can substitute independent effort, it was associated with procrastination and memory loss, alongside poorer academic performance.
text.formatted: There seems to be an "efficiency-understanding" trade-off among learners. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abbas et al. (2024)</ref> showed that, when students realized that AI assistance can substitute independent effort, it was associated with procrastination and memory loss, alongside poorer academic performance.

text.text: The findings in the literature seem to point in the direction that the undesirable influences of AI use on learners mainly take place in the psychological and motivational levels.
Importantly, previous findings showing the associations between AI use and diminished engagement entail further exploration on what carries them.
If AI use is linked with decreased effort, this potential correlation is unlikely to be direct since tool use is a behavior and not a motive.

A plausible account is that the use of AI is related to changes in core motivational appraisals such as whether the authentic learning is still worth doing oneself, and whether one can still do it without AI assistance.
Testing such an indirect path requires measures of learning value and self-efficacy explicitly situated in the AI context.
The field lacks the tools to examine these dynamics.

At first glance, it might be tempting to think that classical self-efficacy and task value measures already account for AI's presence, since today's students necessarily complete the MSLQ as learners already embedded in an AIrich environment.
However, classical measures (e.g., MSLQ; Pintrich et al., 1991) assess the value of completing a course or domain and the self-efficacy of the learner within it.
text.formatted: However, classical measures (e.g., MSLQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Pintrich et al., 1991)</ref> assess the value of completing a course or domain and the self-efficacy of the learner within it.

text.text: They do not question one's personal capability for learning and the value of it when a tool can complete the required tasks.

Classical scales may therefore fail to differentiate between two forms of learning: one in which the learner completes the expected tasks, possibly by letting AI do them, versus one in which the learner values and feels capable of their personal understanding and learning in spite of the significant shortcuts that AI can provide.
The question that remains open is whether this conceptual distinction translates into empirically separable constructs.
It is yet to be tested whether appraisals of value and capability that are explicitly AI-contextualized are different from the classical, AI-unspecified appraisals.
Current instruments measure aspects such as AI literacy among learners, or how much learners feel capable in their use of AI, or their motivation for learning AI.
These instruments are mainly intended to study AI as the objective and outcome of education.
What is missing is an arguably more fundamental measurement which is intended to measure learning motivation as an outcome where AI is the context.

In this study, we explore whether appraisals of task value and self-efficacy, when explicitly situated in the context of AI availability, are empirically distinguishable from their classical counterparts, and then we introduce and validate two brief measurements for two main constructs: Learning Value in the Context of AI and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI.
It will be done with a large sample of traditional-age and adult undergraduate students.
The two AI-related constructs that are the focus of this study are derived from two motivational components at the center of expectancy-value theory.

In expectancy-value theory and its later updated situated version (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002 , 2020), achievement behavior is motivated by two questions on the mind of the learner: "Can I do this task?"
text.formatted: In expectancy-value theory and its later updated situated version <ref type="bibr">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">, 2020)</ref>, achievement behavior is motivated by two questions on the mind of the learner: "Can I do this task?"

text.text: (expectation of success) and "Do I want to do this task, and why?"
(subjective value).

The four compartments of the appraised subjective value include intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value, and cost, which result in how valuable a task or an outcome seems in the eyes of a learner.
This dynamic can potentially be fundamentally impacted in a learning environment where generative AI can help perform the educational tasks and prepare related outcomes.

Realizing that durable learning is no longer the only way for students to perform and accomplish, along with the fact that there is a new convenient way that speeds up progress can truly impact how meaningful learning is, with all four theoretical aspects of "value" being impacted.
The four components of value are not necessarily impacted in the same way when AI is present in the learning context.
Utility value seems to be the most vulnerable one.
The reason is the appraised instrumental payoff of learning a skill can decrease when the tasks associated with that skill can be performed by AI.
Similarly, the cost component is aggravated, since the time and effort invested in durable learning might feel less justified considering the faster path.
Intrinsic and attainment values could be diminished less, as they are tied to the personal meaning and the identity relevance of learning.
However, these two value dimensions of learning can be diminished in more gradual forms, since people's hierarchy of values could shift towards valuing AI-skills.
Here, Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI) can be defined as the perceived value of learning knowledge and skills in a context where AI tools can perform the associated tasks.
Hence, LV-AI is not about what a learner believes about AI, it is the new belief of the learner towards learning when AI's shortcut-like facilitations are present.
The other main question, "Can I do this task?"
relates to learners' expectations of success and their appraisals of personal capability, a component closely aligned with self-efficacy as described in social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1997).
text.formatted: relates to learners' expectations of success and their appraisals of personal capability, a component closely aligned with self-efficacy as described in social cognitive theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bandura, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research has repeatedly shown that self-efficacy is among the strongest predictors of academic success (Schneider & Preckel, 2017).
text.formatted: Previous research has repeatedly shown that self-efficacy is among the strongest predictors of academic success <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Schneider & Preckel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The introduction of generative AI has equipped many learners with an enhanced sense of capability and confidence when performing learning tasks and pursuing educational goals.
However, the increased use of this tool has been found as associated with AI dependency, which is in turn associated with weakened critical thinking (Tian & Zhang, 2025).
text.formatted: However, the increased use of this tool has been found as associated with AI dependency, which is in turn associated with weakened critical thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Tian & Zhang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It seems to be indicative of a shift from productive tool use to problematic reliance.

To clearly address this phenomenon, we explore Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI) defined as a learner's appraisal of their ability to learn and perform academically, without relying on AI tools.

During recent years, different psychometrics measurements have been developed for the assessment of several AI-related features, mainly including literacy, self-efficacy, and competence for using generative AI.

The Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES) developed by Wang and Chuang (2024) measures 4 subcategory of confidence in one's ability to use AI including "assistance, anthropomorphic interaction, comfort with AI, and technological skills."
text.formatted: The Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES) developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Wang and Chuang (2024)</ref> measures 4 subcategory of confidence in one's ability to use AI including "assistance, anthropomorphic interaction, comfort with AI, and technological skills."

text.text: Other developed scales are aimed at measuring AI competence self-efficacy (Chiu, Ahmad, & Çoban, 2025; Chiu et al., 2025) and readiness to learn AI (e.g., the AI Learning Readiness Self-Efficacy scale; Oksanen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Other developed scales are aimed at measuring AI competence self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Chiu, Ahmad, & Çoban, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chiu et al., 2025)</ref> and readiness to learn AI (e.g., the AI Learning Readiness Self-Efficacy scale; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Oksanen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In all these scales, the capable self is one in which the learner feels more capable of using AI well.
However, LSE-AI in this study inverts this referent.
The question becomes whether the learner is confident in their individual capability of learning independently even when AI tools are available.
There is also a second group of AI-related educational measurements, which address how much a learner is motivated to learn AI.

For example, AI Motivation Scale (AIMS; Li et al. 2025) uses the lens of self-determination and measures motivation to learn with AI in terms of intrinsic, identified, introjected, and external regulation and amotivation.
text.formatted: For example, AI Motivation Scale (AIMS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Li et al. 2025</ref>) uses the lens of self-determination and measures motivation to learn with AI in terms of intrinsic, identified, introjected, and external regulation and amotivation.

text.text: In this measurement, the focus is the learner's engagement with AI as a tool, rather than the value of learning itself when AI is available.
To the best of authors' knowledge, the scale that is the closest to the present work is the AI-Motivation and Needs scale (AIM-N; Maska et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To the best of authors' knowledge, the scale that is the closest to the present work is the AI-Motivation and Needs scale (AIM-N; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Maska et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This scale measures the degree to which a learner perceives learning tasks and degree pursuit as redundant and unnecessary due to the existence of AI and how it can substitute the educational endeavors.
While such redundancy beliefs are conceptually close to the Learning Value in the Context of AI, there are important distinctions between these two constructs.

While the redundancy beliefs involve how much AI tools make learning endeavors obsolete and substituted, LV-AI refers to how much these learning activities that lead to deeper development of understanding are still valuable.
A learner can consider a skill redundant while still appraising its acquisition as intensely valuable, or vice versa.
Moreover, they are grounded theoretically in a different way.
While the AIM-N originated in the self-determination theory and its account of need satisfaction, LV-AI is grounded in expectancy-value theory's account of subjective task value.
The distinction between the AI-contextualized vs. classical task value and self-efficacy lies in the condition where the motivational appraisals take place.
Two features of the added clause explain why the appraisals may come apart.
First, value judgments are comparative.
Asking whether learning is important invokes the alternative of not learning, which few learners endorse.
Asking whether learning is worth it when AI can perform the task invokes the alternative of delegating, which is available, fast, and effective.

Second, that comparison is largely a question of cost -the time and effort durable learning requires relative to the shorter route -and cost is the value dimension least represented in classical task value measures.
A parallel logic applies to capability.

Efficacy appraisals rest heavily on prior mastery experience, and for current students much of that experience has been AI-assisted; asking about capability without AI therefore asks learners to judge themselves against evidence they may have less of.
The distinction rests on what each appraisal takes as its object.
Classical task value asks how much a learner values a course or domain; LV-AI asks how much a learner values personally acquiring the capability when a substitute for that capability exists.
These are logically independent: a student may regard a program as highly valuable for their career while doubting that they need to learn its content themselves.
Classical self-efficacy asks whether a learner expects to succeed in their program; LSE-AI asks whether they can learn and perform without leaning on AI.
Success and unaided capability come apart precisely when a capable tool is available.
Moreover, classical instruments were developed before generative AI was available to students, so their items leave the tool context unspecified and respondents supply it themselves.
A classical score is therefore ambiguous about whether AI availability was considered at all, which is what an explicitly AI-situated item removes.
To summarize, the current measurements are mainly designed to assess learners' motivation for learning how to use AI.

They do not examine AI-situated self-efficacy and task value which are the two constructs that gain significant meaning in this new educational era while grounded in expectancy-value theory and social cognitive theory as the core motivational features in learning.

To explore the newly situated learning motivation, compare it across groups, and study related interventions, there is the need for developing scales that can measure the value of and confidence in learning when AI can do the work.
Such a need becomes more salient considering the increasing evidence outlining the corroding effects of AI reliance (Fan et al., 2025; Tian & Zhang, 2025).
text.formatted: Such a need becomes more salient considering the increasing evidence outlining the corroding effects of AI reliance <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Tian & Zhang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Considering that a large portion of motivational studies take place within the context of undergraduate students, comparing the function of a new instrument among traditional-aged and adult undergraduate students provides insights into the consistency of the measurement.
Commonly defined as students aged 25 and older, adult learners experience different educational paths when compared with traditional-aged students.
Such differences exist in terms of role demands, responsibilities associated with being an adult, needs, motivational profiles, and educational histories.
These differences can plausibly be relevant to both of the present constructs.

While the applications of AI in adult education contexts have increased (Yazdani et al., 2025), the fact that adults have for a longer time experienced pre-AI life (at the time this study is conducted) can be reflected in how they view and judge AI-independent learning, both in terms of capability and value.
text.formatted: While the applications of AI in adult education contexts have increased <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Yazdani et al., 2025)</ref>, the fact that adults have for a longer time experienced pre-AI life (at the time this study is conducted) can be reflected in how they view and judge AI-independent learning, both in terms of capability and value.

text.text: The present study tests configural, metric, and scalar invariance across traditional-age and adult learners, using a sample recruited to represent both age groups in approximately equal numbers.

In this study we examine whether appraisals of academic task value and self-efficacy when explicitly situated in the context of AI availability are different from the classical counter, developing and validating the Learning Value in the Context of AI and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI scales in a sample of 882 undergraduate students in the United States of America.

The steps taken for the validation process involve exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, reliability estimation, convergent validity, discriminant validity against classical task value and self-efficacy, measurement invariance across student type, and criterion validity.

To examine the criterion validity of the Learning Value in the Context of AI and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI scales, we explore the predictive power of these two constructs for three academic outcome variables including effort expenditure, persistence, and GPA.

The predictive power of the two AI-situated motivational variables is examined above and beyond classical task value and self-efficacy, student age type (adult or traditional undergraduate), and frequency of AI use.
Exploring the incremental prediction reveals whether the two AI-contextualized motivational beliefs meaningfully add information that the classical self-efficacy and task value do not already carry.

Because existing work has not examined what accounts for the association between AI use and academic engagement, we adopt an exploratory basis to explore whether LV-AI and LSE-AI help explain that potential association.
Guided by the above, the present study addresses the following research questions: RQ1.
Do appraisals of task value and self-efficacy, when explicitly situated in the context of AI availability, form empirically distinguishable factors?
Are the resulting scales internally consistent, and do they demonstrate convergent validity as well as discriminant validity both from one another and from classical task value and self-efficacy?
RQ3.
Do the scales function similarly across traditional-age and adult undergraduate students?
RQ4.

Do LV-AI and LSE-AI predict academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence intention, and GPA) above and beyond classical task value, classical self-efficacy, student age type, and frequency of AI use?
Provided that AI use is associated with academic outcomes, to what extent are these associations accounted for indirectly through LV-AI and LSE-AI?
Data were initially collected from 897 undergraduate students through the online research and data collection platform Prolific in March 2026.
For the participant to be eligible to participate in the study, they had to be enrolled in an undergraduate program in the United States.
To ensure that data were representative of both age groups, we recruited approximately similar numbers of participants from each age group.
After data cleaning, which will be later described, the final sample included 882 participants with 471 traditional-age students and 410 adult students (there was one case where the age was missing).
Participants' age ranged from 18 to 69 years old (M = 27.09).
The data collection of this study was done as a part of a bigger survey.
Each participant was compensated with 6 dollars for their participation.
Of the 882 participants, 53.4% were traditional-age students under 25 years of age and 46.5% were adult learners.
Regarding gender, there were 463 (52.5%) female, 385 male (43.7%) participants with 24 (2.7%) identifying as non-binary, and 10 preferring not to share.

Regarding race and ethnicity, 425 (48.2%) were White, 153 (17.3%) were Black or African American, 117 (13.3%) as two or more races or ethnicities, 97 (11.0%) as Asian, 69 (7.8%) as Hispanic, 8 (0.9%) as another race or ethnicity, 3 (0.3%) as Middle Eastern or North African, and 2 (0.2%) as American Indian or Alaska Native, while 8 (0.9%) preferred not to say.

Participants were from different fields of study including engineering or computer science (n = 214, 24.3%), business or management (n = 189, 21.4%), social sciences (n = 133, 15.1%), health sciences (n = 119, 13.5%), humanities (n = 90, 10.2%), natural sciences (n = 85, 9.6%), education (n = 29, 3.3%), and law (n = 22, 2.5%). 330 participants (37.4%) were first-generation students.
Participants completed the online survey on Qualtrics, where they were initially informed about the aims and general characteristics of the study and asked to provide their informed consent.

Data were collected for Learning Value in the Context of AI, Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI, AI use, classical task value, classical self-efficacy, effort expenditure, GPA, and persistence intention, along with demographic items.
We designed and administered the survey for this research.
The instrument also included measures of additional constructs that are not reported in this manuscript.

Considering that the whole survey was larger, we embedded five attention checks throughout the questionnaires so that participants' attentiveness to the study and the quality of their data could be ensured.
Participants who failed two or more out of the five attention checks were excluded.
Moreover, we excluded the fastest 5% of the participants with one attention check or straightlining patterns.
Straightlining was defined as repeatedly choosing the same response for 20+ consecutive items.
These exclusion criteria led to filtering 15 individuals, yielding 882 participants as the final sample.
The LV-AI and LSE-AI scales were developed through an iterative process.
To start, the general definition and specific aspects of the constructs were prepared by the first author.
Next, a generative AI tool (ChatGPT; OpenAI) was used to assist with the preparation of candidate items based on our specifications for the two constructs.
It was followed by the evaluation and revision of the candidate items for construct validity.
We assessed items for clarity and for framing AI comprehensively (not being limited to one generative AI tool).
Finally, a short pilot study involved 28 participants completing the survey study and 3 of them providing qualitative feedback.

The completions did not show signs of fundamental and technical flaws in the online survey, and the qualitative feedback was not indicative of any major issues that were troublesome for participants when comprehending and answering the scales.

Considering the importance of how academic AI use can be associated with changes in learners' motivational dynamics, the present study introduced and validated two brief scales for the measurement of two focal learning motivational constructs in AI-rich educational contexts.

These two constructs include Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI), referring to the perceived value of acquiring knowledge and skills when AI tools can perform the associated tasks, and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI), described as the learner's perceived capability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI.
The study was performed while also exploring and comparing the applicability of the scales among adult (above 25-years of age) vs. traditional-age (between 18-25 years of age) undergraduate students.

Identified by exploratory factor analysis and supported by confirmatory factor analysis, the suggested two-factor structure comprising three items per construct showed excellent model fit, acceptable internal consistency, and obvious superiority over one-factor and orthogonal alternatives.
The results were indicative of the two scales being empirically distinguishable from each other (HTMT = .84) and from classical task value and self-efficacy.

The scales also showed configural and metric invariance and partial scalar invariance across traditional-age and adult learners, and incremental prediction of persistence intention and effort expenditure beyond classical motivational constructs, student type, and frequency of AI use.

Overall, the results support that the two scales are psychometrically sound instruments for studying Learning Value in the Context of AI and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI as motivational consequences of AI in higher education.
There are a number of theoretical implications that the findings highlight.

Firstly, the two AI constructs could significantly predict effort expenditure (ΔR² = .022, with both constructs contributing independently) and persistence intention (ΔR² = .015, driven primarily by LV-AI), but not GPA.
Consistent with the previous studies, effort and persistence are the direct proximal behavioral expressions of motivation according to expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Consistent with the previous studies, effort and persistence are the direct proximal behavioral expressions of motivation according to expectancy-value theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, GPA is a distal outcome influenced by more non-motivational determinants (e.g., prior achievement, course difficulty).

The AI-contextualized motivational beliefs are mainly drivers of energization and direction of motivated learning behavior rather than graded performance, which is expected to be indirectly and less strongly improved by motivational beliefs.
The strongest predictor of GPA among the motivational beliefs was classical selfefficacy, which is an observation consistent with previous findings (Schneider & Preckel, 2017).
text.formatted: The strongest predictor of GPA among the motivational beliefs was classical selfefficacy, which is an observation consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Schneider & Preckel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Secondly, while the two AI-influenced motivational constructs were empirically distinguishable, they were strongly correlated at the latent level (r = .85).
Expectancy value theory highlights expectancy and value as two distinct constructs with reciprocity in how they influence belief systems.

The strong link between LV-AI and LSE-AI shows that when students doubt the value of durable learning when AI quickly provides access to the academic products, they also feel less capable of learning those skills without AI.
The opposite trend also holds true, meaning that declining confidence in one's capability to learn without relying on AI undermines the perceived value of durable learning.
Whether any of these two constructs are causally prior can be studied using longitudinal designs.

Third and relatedly, the four-factor model tested in this study showed that the two AI constructs are not redundant with their classical counterparts, considering that merging each of them with its classical counterpart resulted in considerably worse fit and that their HTMT values with the classical constructs were low.

It suggests that situating task value and self-efficacy in an AI-rich context does not simply reproduce the classical constructs, but rather captures motivational beliefs that the classical measures do not already carry.
Finally, the invariance results show that the scales function equivalently at the configural and metric levels among both the traditional-age and adult learners, except for one Learning
Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI item.
The age group seemed to lead to different baseline endorsements of the item "When learning tasks are challenging, I can rely on my own abilities rather than depending entirely on AI tools."
This deviation in how the two age groups treat the item is very much interpretable, especially considering that this is the only item measuring learners' reaction to when tasks become challenging.
Adult learners tend to make judgments about themselves based on longer time periods (decades) of pre-AI contexts where academic and educational tasks needed to be handled without the help of AI.
It provided them with more volume of independent master experience, hence the shift in the item's endorsement without altering the construct's meaning.
Since five of six intercepts were invariant, latent comparisons across student age groups remain defensible.

The inverse associations that AI use had with LV-AI and LSE-AI are important findings bearing significant insights regarding the learning motivational dynamics of the current AI-rich educational context.
The fact that both of the AI constructs were negatively correlated with AI use (LV-AI: r = -.30; LSE-AI: r = -.32) can be interpreted differently.

An initial interpretation can be that, when AI is introduced in educational contexts, students who feel value in learning per-se and feel capable in learning independent of AI tend to use this tool less.

On the other hand, the other conceivable trend is that when students use generative AI for their educational endeavors, they tend to feel that the completion of these tasks through the more effortful durable learning is not worth it.
Such a decrease in the appraisal of value can also be the result of comparing the two ways of achieving the academic goal in terms of their costs (emotional, time, effort).

Moreover, the efficiency of AI task accomplishment can make the learner think that "this close-to-perfect job done so quickly by AI would have been of less quality and more flaw if I wanted to do myself, which would have taken much longer and more effortful."

In addition to time and effort, the emotional cost is another issue which one faces when one chooses the durable learning path (please note that, now, this learner has thoughts about the possibility of another easier path, an image that aggravates the cost imbalance).
The emerging literature also suggests that heavy AI use may erode these beliefs over time (Fan et al., 2025; Tian & Zhang, 2025).

text.text: It still should be highlighted that these cross-sectional associations cannot adjudicate direction in a certain way before further evidence is observed.

The results of the present findings can be accounted for by the previously mentioned potential dynamics, or they could be only indicative of students using AI less because they value and trust their own learning or a combination of the two.
Both readings are supported by the data, and further research to distinguish them is among the most important questions these scales now make tractable.
It is important to explore the role of AI use when the new AI-contextualized motivational constructs are modeled.
In the hierarchical regression analyses and before modeling LV-AI and LSE-AI, the relationship between AI use and effort expenditure was significant.
However, after the two constructs were entered, it fell to non-significance.
Exploratory path modeling was performed to explore the mediating effects of LV-AI and LSE-AI on the relationship between AI use and effort.
It showed that just over half of the AI use's total association with effort expenditure was carried indirectly through the two constructs, with no significant direct path remaining.
With cautious interpretation, this suggests that the negative association between AI use and effort expenditure is largely shared with the two AI-embedded motivational beliefs here.
There are at least two ways of explaining these findings.
On the one hand, it can be the case that frequent academic use of generative AI can lead to the erosion of learners' appraisal of value and self-efficacy in AI-independent learning.
On the other hand, it is possible that students who already place little value on learning without AI may both turn to AI more often and invest less effort.
In this way, AI use and effort are joint expressions of an already existing motivational stance rather than links in a causal chain.
Considering the cross-sectional design of the study, the results are supportive of an indirect pathway but do not establish causality.
Future studies with longitudinal and experimental designs can explore these possible accounts and the scales suggested in this paper can be used for that purpose.
The observed pattern has a consequential interpretation.
It seems that once the learners' motivational beliefs in AI-embedded educational contexts are known, their degree of AI use has little further information to add about their effort.
This has a direct practical implication.

For decision-makers, institutions, and educators who are mainly worried about the degree of AI use among learners, the findings of this study warn them about being concerned about measuring the wrong thing.

Instead, it points them towards the potentially more important and decisive role of learners' AI-contextualized motivational belief about learning, here being the value of learning and the confidence in one's capability to learn AI-independently.
This perspective seems to be more effective when trying to enhance learners' engagement and effort in the new AI-saturated educational era.
Since each of the constructs have three items, the brevity of the scales makes them practical for using in institutional and classroom settings.
As evaluation instruments, these scales can be used by institutions that adopt new AI tools and policies to monitor the motivational correlates of those decisions.
Data collected before and after such decisions and policy changes can provide them with such insights.
In addition to such practical uses, future research can also use these scales in order to explore the correlations and intervention effects in the context of AIrelated motivational research.

Finally, considering that findings show that both LV-AI and LSE-AI predict increased effort and persistence, which are important academic decisions and behaviors, this study can provide educators with insights regarding how reliance on generative AI can be associated with decreased academic persistence (withdrawal) and effort (disengagement).

Addressing unfavorable previous findings about AI use and disengagement in learning, the findings of this study suggest that the practical aim is not less AI use, but AI use that leaves the value of and confidence in one's own learning intact.
There were several limitations in this study.
Firstly, this study was cross-sectional.
Future studies with multiple data points or longitudinal designs can put the criterion validity of the scales to the test in a more detailed way.
Moreover, the fact that this study relied on self-reported data is another limitation of this study.

For the LSE-AI scale, while all loadings were significant and substantial and the composite reliability was found to be adequate, the average variance extracted was slightly lower (.46) than the conventional .50 criterion.
The fact that the scale consists of 3 items can make the .50 AVE criterion rather too conservative for such a brief scale.
However, the AVE can be increased in longer versions of this scale where more items are added.
Relatedly, the brevity of the scale can be preventing in terms of detailed measurement of subconstructs.
For example, the fourth dimensions of task value (especially cost) can be more meticulously assessed if more targeted items are included in future scales.
Future versions of LV-AI and LSE-AI scales that are longer and more constructually comprehensive can benefit from further structured content validation.

Finally, although the sample was large and deliberately balanced across two age groups, replicating similar studies in different cultural contexts can help explore the generalizable vs. unique findings.

In terms of theoretical coverage, item 1 involves the general appraisal of capability when AI tools are available, item 2 addresses the capability of developing understanding beyond what AI initially provides, and item 3 is reflective of efficacy appraisal when tasks become challenging.
AI Use.

AI Use was measured using four items to control for the variance in the general AI engagement when the predictive power of LV-AI and LSE-AI for the academic outcome variables were examined in criterion validity analyses.
On a 5-point Likert scale, participants indicated how frequent the items were true about them (from "1" meaning "very rarely/never" to "5" meaning "very often").

The items include: "I use AI tools as a student"; "I use AI tools for my learning activities"; "I use AI tools to fulfil my academic responsibilities"; and "I use AI tools to perform my academic assignments."

AI tools are now a permanent feature of the educational landscape, which raises the question of what their presence does to learners' motivation.
Answering these questions requires instruments that can be used to measure motivational qualities about learning that are situated in AI-rich contexts.

For this purpose, the Learning Value in the Context of AI and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI scales suggested in the present study provide brief and psychometrically validated tools that are theoretically grounded.
The findings of this study indicate their prediction of academic effort and persistence, their equivalence across traditionalage and adult learners, and their negative relationships with AI use.
It establishes a foundation for the required future research exploring the motivational consequences of AI in education and learning.
